breadseed-poppy.cleaning: Pour the seed through a fine sieve, or blow gently across it, to lift out bits of pod and dust. Pick out any pale, soft seed.
breadseed-poppy.drying: Spread the seed thin on a tray or screen in a dry, airy spot for a few days, until it is hard and fully dry, before you jar it.
breadseed-poppy.how_to_collect: Cut the dry pods and tip them over a bowl or bucket. The ripe seed pours out through the little holes that open under the crown of the pod, like a pepper shaker.
breadseed-poppy.pollination_notes: Bees work the flowers and varieties cross readily, so grow only one variety, or keep varieties about 300 feet apart, for seed that comes true.
breadseed-poppy.storage: Keep in a sealed jar in a cool, dark, dry place. Poppy seed is short-lived — plan on about 2 years.
breadseed-poppy.when_to_harvest: Wait until the pods have dried on the plant and turned tan. Give a pod a shake — when the seeds rattle inside, they are ripe.

calendula.cleaning: Shake out loose petal bits and blow off the light chaff. Pick out any soft, green seed.
calendula.drying: Spread the seed in a single layer in a dry, airy place for 3 to 7 days, up to a week or two, until a seed snaps rather than bends.
calendula.how_to_collect: Rub or brush the dry heads over a bowl and the crescent seeds come away easily. Heads picked a touch green will finish ripening as they dry.
calendula.pollination_notes: Calendula mostly pollinates itself and crossing is uncommon, but bees can carry pollen between varieties. Grow one variety, or keep varieties about 700 feet apart, for seed that comes true.
calendula.storage: Store in an envelope or jar in a cool, dark, dry place. Calendula seed is best sown within a few years — figure on about 3 years of good life, sometimes longer.
calendula.when_to_harvest: The seeds ripen fast and drop quickly, so check plants often. Pick heads as they turn brown and tan, while the curved, crescent-shaped seeds are still held in the head — or slip a small bag over ripening heads to catch what falls.

celosia.cleaning: Shake the seed out and winnow or sieve away the papery husks and dust. The seed is tiny, so work over a tray or cloth to catch it.
celosia.drying: Hang the cut heads in a dry, airy place until they are fully crisp, then thresh the seed out and give it a final airing before storing.
celosia.how_to_collect: Cut the whole heads and hang them to dry a little further, then shake and rub them over a bowl or screen so the little black seeds fall free of the papery husks.
celosia.pollination_notes: Celosia pollinates itself, but insects cross varieties too, so keep varieties about a quarter mile apart for pure seed.
celosia.storage: Store in a sealed jar or envelope in a cool, dark, dry place. Celosia seed keeps about 4 years in good storage.
celosia.when_to_harvest: Wait until the seeds inside the heads have dried and start to drop on their own. The tiny, glossy black seeds collect at the base of the papery flower heads.

cornflower.cleaning: Rub the heads apart, then winnow in front of a low fan, or blow across the seed, to lift off the light chaff.
cornflower.drying: Bring the heads in and let them cure 1 to 2 weeks, then rub the seed out and give it a couple more days of airing before storing.
cornflower.how_to_collect: Cut the dry heads into a paper bag on a dry day. Rub the top of each head between your palms and the seeds roll out.
cornflower.pollination_notes: Open-pollinated cornflowers come true, but bees cross the colours, so a mixed patch gives mixed colours. Seed from F1 hybrids will not grow true.
cornflower.storage: Keep in paper envelopes in a cool, dark, dry place. Cornflower seed stays good for a few years.
cornflower.when_to_harvest: Let the heads dry on the plant until they are brown, with a furry centre. The ripe seeds are small tan barrels with a little tuft of bristles.

cosmos.cleaning: Rub the heads apart and pick out the firm, dark seeds, discarding soft or green ones. Blow off the light chaff.
cosmos.drying: Spread the seed in a single layer in a dry place. It can take several weeks to dry all the way through — be patient before storing.
cosmos.how_to_collect: On a dry day, snip the ripening heads straight into a bag so nothing drops. Rub the heads over a screen to free the seed.
cosmos.pollination_notes: Bees cross cosmos, so keep varieties about a quarter mile apart for pure seed. The two garden species, Cosmos bipinnatus and Cosmos sulphureus, usually don't cross with each other.
cosmos.storage: Keep in a sealed jar or envelope in a cool, dark, dry place. Cosmos seed stays viable about 5 years in good storage.
cosmos.when_to_harvest: The seed ripens fast and shatters, so watch the heads closely and pick each one as it ripens. Ripe seeds are the slender, dark, double-pointed sticks in the centre of the spent head — a ripe one flicks loose easily.

echinacea.cleaning: The seed is heavier than the chaff, so blow across it, or pour it in front of a fan, and the light bits lift away. Pick out any soft or pale seed.
echinacea.drying: If the cones feel at all damp, spread or hang them in a dry, airy place for 2 to 3 weeks to finish drying before you rub the seed out.
echinacea.how_to_collect: Cut the dry cones into a paper bag before they shatter and drop their seed. Rub the cones hard between your palms, or shake the heads in a lidded can, to knock the seed free.
echinacea.pollination_notes: The common garden species are open-pollinated and come true when grown on their own, but the species cross with each other and hybrids pop up — grow one kind by itself for true seed.
echinacea.storage: Store in a sealed jar in a cool, dark, dry place. In good storage it stays viable about 2 to 3 years.
echinacea.when_to_harvest: Let the cones dry on the plant until they are dark brown to black, crisp, and prickly. Rub a cone with a gloved thumb — ripe seed loosens and starts to come away.

larkspur.cleaning: Pour the seed through a sieve and blow off the pod bits. Pick out any pale or shrivelled seed.
larkspur.drying: Let the stalks finish drying indoors for about two weeks after cutting, then thresh, and give the seed a final airing before storing.
larkspur.how_to_collect: Cut whole stalks at the rattle stage and bring them indoors. Dry them about two more weeks, then shake or rub the seed out of the pods into a container.
larkspur.pollination_notes: The flowers are open to insects and varieties cross, so grow only one variety if you want pure seed. All parts of larkspur, including the seed, are poisonous — keep saved seed labelled and away from children and livestock.
larkspur.storage: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dark, dry place. Larkspur seed is short-lived — sow it fresh, within a year or two.
larkspur.when_to_harvest: Watch the pods as they swell, turn brown, and dry on the stalk. Cut when the seeds rattle inside the pods, but before the pods split and spill.

marigold.cleaning: Pull the seed bundles apart and shake out loose bits of petal and cup. There is little chaff; just pick out any soft or green seed.
marigold.drying: Spread the seed out for a few days, up to 1 to 2 weeks, until it is fully dry before storing.
marigold.how_to_collect: Pull the dry heads and squeeze or pull them apart over a bowl. The seeds — slim black sticks with a pale tip, like tiny paintbrushes — fall right out.
marigold.pollination_notes: Marigolds pollinate themselves, but bees can cross varieties, so keep varieties about a quarter mile apart for pure seed. Seed saved from hybrids will not grow true to the parent plant.
marigold.storage: Keep in an envelope or jar in a cool, dark, dry place. Marigold seed stays viable about 5 years in good storage.
marigold.when_to_harvest: Let the heads dry completely on the plant, until they are brown, papery, and shrivelled. Inside each dried cup sits a bundle of ripe seed.

nigella.cleaning: Pour the seed through a sieve and blow or winnow off the light pod flakes. Spread it out and pick over any green or soft seed.
nigella.drying: Spread the seed in a thin layer indoors for about a week, until it is hard and dry.
nigella.how_to_collect: Snip the dry pods into a paper bag, or cut the stems and hang them upside down over a sheet. Crush or shake the pods and the black seed falls out through the opening at the top.
nigella.pollination_notes: Bees cross the colours freely, so a mixed patch gives mixed colours in the seed you save. Keep one variety about a quarter mile from others for pure seed.
nigella.storage: Store in a paper envelope or sealed jar in a cool, dark, dry place. Expect it to stay good for roughly 2 to 5 years.
nigella.when_to_harvest: Let the pods dry on the plant until they turn papery and buff-tan and the stripes fade. Shake one — ripe seed rattles inside the crunchy, balloon-like pod.

pincushion-flower.cleaning: Rub the heads over a screen, then winnow by pouring the seed in front of a gentle fan, or blowing across it, to carry off the chaff.
pincushion-flower.drying: Spread the cleaned seed thin in a dry, airy place until it is fully dry and hard before storing.
pincushion-flower.how_to_collect: Cut the dry heads straight into a paper bag so you don't lose seed on the way. Rub or crush the heads between your hands to free the seed from its little compartments.
pincushion-flower.pollination_notes: Insects cross scabiosa readily, so grow one variety at a time, or isolate varieties, to keep seed true. Seed from hybrid varieties will not grow true to the parent.
pincushion-flower.storage: Keep in a sealed jar or envelope in a cool, dark, dry place. In good storage it stays viable up to about 3 years.
pincushion-flower.when_to_harvest: Leave the heads on the plant until they are fully dry and brown or tan. Start picking as soon as the first seeds begin to loosen and shatter — wait too long and the rest drops.

strawflower.cleaning: Rub the heads to release the seed, then blow or winnow off the fluff and chaff. Pick out any soft seed.
strawflower.drying: Air-dry the heads 7 to 10 days in a dry spot, before or after rubbing the seed out, until everything is crisp and dry.
strawflower.how_to_collect: Cut the fully dry heads and rub them between your hands over a bowl. The ripe seed shakes loose from the fluffy centre.
strawflower.pollination_notes: Strawflowers mostly pollinate themselves, but insects can carry pollen between varieties. Open-pollinated varieties come true as long as they don't share pollen with another variety nearby.
strawflower.storage: Keep in a sealed jar or envelope in a cool, dark, dry place. Strawflower seed is fairly short-lived — plan on about 2 years.
strawflower.when_to_harvest: Leave some heads on the plant well past their pretty stage, until the papery bracts are fully dry and the centre of the head turns fluffy, like a tiny dandelion clock.

sunflower.cleaning: Rub the seeds loose and pour them in front of a fan to winnow away the light chaff. Pick out any soft or empty seeds.
sunflower.drying: Hang cut heads upside down in a dry, airy spot for 1 to 2 weeks, until the seeds rub out easily and feel hard and dry.
sunflower.how_to_collect: Slip a paper bag over ripening heads to keep the birds off. Cut the head with a length of stem and hang it upside down in a dry, airy place for 1 to 2 weeks, then rub the seeds out by hand.
sunflower.pollination_notes: Bees cross sunflowers freely, so keep varieties about half a mile apart for pure seed. Save seed only from open-pollinated or heirloom kinds — hybrid (F1) seed will not grow true.
sunflower.storage: Store in a sealed jar or envelope in a cool, dark, dry place. Sunflower seed keeps about 1 to 3 years, losing strength as it ages — sow the freshest first.
sunflower.when_to_harvest: The back of the head turns from green to yellow to brown, the petals drop, and the head hangs heavy and droops. The seeds should be plump, firm, and fully striped.

sweet-pea.cleaning: Shell the peas out and pick over them, tossing any shrivelled or discoloured seed. The seed is big, so there is little chaff to deal with.
sweet-pea.drying: Spread the shelled seed in a dry, warm spot and let it dry further, until it is hard, before you store it.
sweet-pea.how_to_collect: Snip the pods off, leaving a few inches of stem on each. Spread them on a screen, or hang them, in a dry, warm place until they split, then shell the seed out by hand.
sweet-pea.pollination_notes: Sweet peas mostly pollinate themselves inside their closed flowers, so varieties usually come true without isolation — but crosses do happen, so saved seed is not guaranteed true.
sweet-pea.storage: Keep in a sealed jar or envelope in a cool, dark, dry place. Stored well, sweet pea seed stays viable about 3 to 5 years.
sweet-pea.when_to_harvest: Leave the pods on the vine until they are brown, dry, and plump. Pick them before they pop open and scatter the seed.

zinnia.cleaning: Winnow with a fan or your breath — the light, papery chaff blows away, and takes immature seed and disease-carrying bits with it. Keep only plump, firm seed.
zinnia.drying: Spread the seed in a thin layer out of direct sun and let it dry at least 3 weeks, stirring it once or twice a day, before storing.
zinnia.how_to_collect: Cut the dry heads and crumble or rub them apart over a tray. The seeds pull free from the dried head.
zinnia.pollination_notes: Zinnias mostly pollinate themselves, and you can bag or cage a few heads to keep them pure. For field seed, grow one variety per season, or keep varieties several hundred feet apart.
zinnia.storage: Store airtight in a cool, dark, dry place. Well-kept zinnia seed stays good for about 5 years.
zinnia.when_to_harvest: Leave the heads on the plant until they are completely dry and brown, and the stem just below the head has browned too. Ripe seed is the stiff, arrowhead-shaped seed at the base of each petal.
